How well can you turn a seemingly negative quality into a positive? I'm about to graduate and have been practicing for interviews. I haven't quite figured out how to respond to this question while maintaining a positive spin.
Milk. Put a gallon in front of me and it'll be gone within an hour or two.

Candy corn and salted peanuts. Greatest weakness known to man.

But seriously, these questions are always silly. It's like a petty chess game where you have to humble brag. One possible answer: "I sometimes try to take on too much at once and I'll find myself having to go into overdrive to accomplish everything on time". If you're going for honesty points, "I'm fresh out of college.. my greatest weakness is inexperience, but I counter that with a thirst for knowledge."

This is always a really vague question. The thing with vagueness is that sometimes it leaves you with no direction to answer the question but it also leaves you really free to decide where to go with it.

My answer to this kind of question would be simply a lack of experience in the field. But I'm very aware of my inexperience and that drives me to consistently learn and grow from the experience and environment I am in. I'm more driven because of it.
I always hated this question during job interviews but never had the balls to say "My inability to answer stupid questions."
You can change being a slow worker into "I put too much effort into the details of things and it makes things take longer than they should sometimes."

I think more interviewers are starting to see through the answers that spin it into something positive, like "I'm too dedicated" or "I sometimes hold myself to higher standards than everyone around me." If I'm interviewing someone and asking this, I'd rather see self-awareness than how they spin something and market it to me.*

What I've typically done is to be honest about a mild negative quality, but make sure that I address how I've been working on it and how I plan on continuing to improve it. Example off the top of my head: "I originally had some difficulty managing up, but in my last position I made it a point to be more vocal with my supervisor about other tasks I was working on to help determine priorities. I think I still have room to improve, but I've definitely gotten better at it and plan on continuing to improve."

*Your mileage may vary depending on industry, position, etc. I'm in consulting with small teams working closely together for some crazy hours, so self-awareness and interpersonal skills are pretty important so I don't want to drive a screwdriver through your eye socket at 1:30am. Professionally speaking, of course.

My last interview I answered by saying that interviews made me extremely nervous for some reason and that it was a strange phenomenon because my background is highly padded with meeting new people and having lots of human interaction on the daily (which is all true).
